gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the big stations' inverters draw 15–58 W with nothing plugged in, more than the 40 W CPAP they ranked. The Solar Lab measured about 36 W idle for the DELTA Pro Ultra X, about 45 W for the DELTA Pro Ultra, about 58 W for the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus and about 15 W for the BLUETTI Elite 300. With the CPAP on the AC outlet and the inverter running all day, that cuts the DELTA Pro Ultra X from ChatGPT's 32 nights to about 10, and leaves the 5,040 Wh Jackery (about 2.9 nights) behind the $1,199 3,014 Wh Elite 300 (about 4.4 nights).
standout_why: I compared four pages. powerstations.reviews/for/cpap (cited) uses a flat 85% efficiency and says the figure is 'an assumption, not a measurement of any model'. ridgewatt.com/best/cpap (cited) uses a flat 0.85 factor. pluginsolarcheck.com/power-stations (cited) lists only capacity and price. None of these three gives an idle or no-load figure for any model. ChatGPT's second answer only warned in general terms that idle draw 'can' shorten runtime, with no numbers. All of them rank nights by capacity alone, which puts the Jackery 5000 Plus third. I could not open the cited EnoughWatts page (certificate error), so I can't say whether it has idle figures.
decides: The DELTA Pro Ultra X ($7,899 at EcoFlow today) still gives the most nights, but about 10 on AC with the inverter on all day, not 32. It has no USB or 12 V outputs, so the CPAP can only run through the inverter. Among the units most shoppers would actually buy, idle draw changes the ranking. The Jackery 5000 Plus's 58 W idle leaves it at about 2.9 nights on AC, while the BLUETTI Elite 300 ($1,199 at BLUETTI) gets about 4.4 nights. That matches the out-of-stock DELTA Pro Ultra (about 4.4 nights, $3,799) for under a third of the price, so it costs about $272 per night against about $760 for the Ultra X. On units that have a 12 V car socket, running the CPAP through ResMed's DC converter with the inverter off avoids the idle loss altogether.

findings.label: CPAP nights per charge on AC, idle included
findings.value: about 10.4 nights (about 20 if the inverter runs only 8 h a night)
findings.source_title: The Solar Lab: EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra X home backup unit
findings.note: Our arithmetic, using ChatGPT's own 40 W × 8 h = 320 Wh per night: 12,288 Wh ÷ (320 + 36 W × 24 h = 1,184 Wh a day) = 10.4. Night-only: 12,288 ÷ (320 + 288) = 20.2. Inverter conversion loss on the 40 W load is not included, so these are upper bounds. ChatGPT said 32 nights. About $760 per night ($7,899 ÷ 10.4).

findings.source_title: The Solar Lab: Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus Review
findings.note: The Solar Lab: 'around 58W per hour when we turned the inverter on and let it run through a full charge without any sort of load'. Nights on AC: 5,040 ÷ (320 + 58 × 24 = 1,712) = 2.9; inverter on 8 h only: 6.4. ChatGPT said 13. The review's spec list includes '1 x 12V car socket', so a DC CPAP converter with the inverter off avoids the idle loss. I have not confirmed this on Jackery's page.
